title: III. The Sufferings Of A Soul, The First Ordeal
paragraphs: And so Mitya sat there, staring wildly at the people around him and not taking in a word they said. Then he sprang up, threw his hands in the air and shouted:
“I’m not guilty! I’m not guilty of that blood! I’m not guilty of my father’s blood.... I meant to kill him, yes. But I’m not guilty. Not I.”
No sooner had he said it than Grushenka burst out from behind the curtain and threw herself at the police captain’s feet.

“It’s my fault! Mine! My wickedness!” she cried in a heartbreaking voice, streaming with tears and stretching her clasped hands out to them. “He did it because of me. I tortured him, I drove him to it. In my wickedness I tortured that poor old man who’s dead, too, and brought him to this! It’s my fault, mine first, mine most, mine!”

“Yes, it’s your fault! You’re the chief criminal! You fury! You harlot! You’re the one most to blame!” shouted the police captain, threatening her with his hand. But he was stopped at once, and firmly. The prosecutor simply grabbed him.
“This is totally out of order, Mihail Makarovitch!” he cried. “You’re plainly obstructing the inquiry.... You’re ruining the case....” He was almost choking.
“Keep to procedure! Keep to procedure!” cried Nikolay Parfenovitch, who was terribly worked up himself. “Otherwise it’s absolutely impossible!...”
“Judge us together!” Grushenka cried wildly, still on her knees. “Punish us together. I’ll go with him now, even to my death!”

“Grusha, my life, my blood, my holy one!” Mitya dropped to his knees beside her and clasped her tight. “Don’t believe her,” he cried. “She’s not guilty of anything, not of any blood, not of anything!”

Afterwards he remembered that several men pulled him away from her by force, that she was led out, and that the next thing he knew he was sitting at the table. The men with the metal plates stood beside him and behind him. Across the table sat the investigating lawyer, Nikolay Parfenovitch, who kept urging him to drink a little water from the glass in front of him.

“It will refresh you, it will calm you. Be calm, don’t be frightened,” the lawyer added, with great politeness. Mitya (he remembered this later) all at once became intensely interested in the lawyer’s big rings, one set with an amethyst, the other with a clear, brilliant yellow stone. Long afterwards he still wondered how those rings had held his attention through all those terrible hours of questioning. He had been quite unable to look away from them or write them off as having nothing to do with his plight. On Mitya’s left sat the prosecutor, in the seat Maximov had taken at the start of the evening. On his right, where Grushenka had been, sat a rosy-cheeked young man in a shabby sort of hunting jacket, with ink and paper before him. This was the lawyer’s secretary, whom he had brought along. The police captain was now standing at the window at the far end of the room, next to Kalganov, who was sitting there.
“Drink some water,” the investigating lawyer said softly, for the tenth time.
“I’ve drunk it, gentlemen, I have ... but ... come, gentlemen, crush me, punish me, decide my fate!” cried Mitya, staring at the lawyer with fixed, terribly wide eyes.
“So you firmly declare that you are not guilty of your father’s death, Fyodor Pavlovitch?” the lawyer asked, softly but insistently.

“I’m not guilty. I’m guilty of the blood of another old man, but not of my father’s. And I weep for it! I killed him, I killed the old man and knocked him down.... But it’s hard to answer for that crime with another one, a terrible murder I didn’t commit.... It’s a terrible accusation, gentlemen, a knockout blow. But who killed my father, who killed him? Who could have killed him, if not I? It’s astonishing, extraordinary, impossible.”
“Yes, who could have killed him?” the lawyer began, but Ippolit Kirillovitch, the prosecutor, glanced at him and addressed Mitya himself.

“You needn’t trouble yourself about the old servant, Grigory Vassilyevitch. He is alive and has recovered. By his own account and yours, you dealt him terrible blows. Yet there seems no doubt that he will live, at least according to the doctor.”

“Alive? He’s alive?” cried Mitya, throwing up his hands. His face lit up. “Lord, thank You for the miracle You’ve worked for me, a sinner and a wrongdoer. That’s the answer to my prayer. I’ve been praying all night.” And he crossed himself three times. He could hardly breathe.
“So we have received from this Grigory evidence about you that is very important, namely that—” The prosecutor was about to go on, but Mitya suddenly leapt out of his chair.
“One minute, gentlemen, for God’s sake, just one minute. I’ll run to her—”
“Excuse me, that is out of the question just now,” Nikolay Parfenovitch almost shrieked. He had jumped up too. The men with the metal plates grabbed Mitya, but he sat back down on his own....

“Gentlemen, what a pity! I only wanted to see her for a minute. I wanted to tell her that it’s washed away, it’s gone, that blood that lay on my heart all night, and that I’m not a murderer now! Gentlemen, she is my betrothed!” he said with rapture and reverence, looking around at them all. “Oh, thank you, gentlemen! In one minute you’ve given me a new life, a new heart!... That old man used to carry me in his arms, gentlemen. He used to bathe me in the tub when I was a three-year-old baby that everyone had abandoned. He was like a father to me!...”
“And so you—” the investigating lawyer began.

“Allow me, gentlemen, just one more minute,” Mitya cut in. He put his elbows on the table and hid his face in his hands. “Let me have a moment to think, let me catch my breath, gentlemen. All this is horribly upsetting, horribly. A man is not a drum, gentlemen!”
“Have a little more water,” murmured Nikolay Parfenovitch.

Mitya took his hands from his face and laughed. His eyes were full of confidence. In one moment he seemed an entirely different man. His whole manner had changed. Once more he was the equal of these men, all of whom he knew, as if they had met the day before at some social gathering, when nothing had happened. We may mention in passing that Mitya had been warmly received at the police captain’s when he first came to town. Later, and especially in the last month, he had hardly visited at all. When the police captain met him in the street, Mitya had noticed that the man frowned and bowed only out of politeness. He knew the prosecutor less well. He did sometimes pay polite calls on the prosecutor’s wife, a nervous and fanciful lady, though he hardly knew why. She always welcomed him kindly and, for some reason, had taken an interest in him to the very last. The investigating lawyer he had not had time to get to know, though he had met him and talked with him twice, each time about women.

“I see you’re a very skillful lawyer, Nikolay Parfenovitch,” cried Mitya, laughing merrily, “but now I can help you. Oh, gentlemen, I feel like a new man, and don’t take offense that I speak to you so plainly and directly. I’m a bit drunk, too, I’ll tell you that frankly. I do believe I’ve had the honor and pleasure of meeting you, Nikolay Parfenovitch, at my kinsman Miüsov’s. Gentlemen, gentlemen, I don’t pretend we’re on equal terms. I understand, of course, in what capacity I sit before you. Oh, of course there’s a horrible suspicion ... hanging over me ... if Grigory has given evidence.... A horrible suspicion! It’s awful, awful, I understand that! But to business, gentlemen. I’m ready, and we’ll be done in one moment. Because, listen, listen, gentlemen! Since I know I’m innocent, we can finish this in a minute. Can’t we? Can’t we?”
Mitya talked a great deal and very fast, nervously and gushingly, as if he truly took his listeners for his best friends.

“So, for now, we will put down that you absolutely deny the charge against you,” said Nikolay Parfenovitch impressively. He leaned toward the secretary and dictated to him in a low voice what to write.

“Write it down? You want to write that down? Well, write it. I agree, I fully agree, gentlemen, only ... you see?... Wait, wait, write this. Of disorderly conduct I am guilty, of violence against a poor old man I am guilty. And there’s something else deep in my heart that I’m guilty of, too—but that you needn’t write down” (he turned suddenly to the secretary). “That’s my private life, gentlemen, that’s no concern of yours, the bottom of my heart, I mean.... But I am not guilty of murdering my old father. That’s a wild idea. A completely wild idea!... I’ll prove it to you, and you’ll be convinced right away.... You’ll laugh, gentlemen. You’ll laugh at your own suspicion!...”

“Be calm, Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” said the investigating lawyer, plainly trying to settle Mitya’s excitement with his own composure. “Before we go on, I would like you, if you are willing to answer, to confirm that you disliked your father, Fyodor Pavlovitch, and that you were forever quarreling with him. Here, at any rate, a quarter of an hour ago, you cried out that you wanted to kill him. ‘I didn’t kill him,’ you said, ‘but I wanted to kill him.’”
“I shouted that? Ach, I may well have, gentlemen! Yes, I’m sorry to say I did want to kill him ... many times I wanted to ... sorry, so sorry!”
“You wanted to. Would you be willing to explain what exactly led you to hate your father so?”

“What is there to explain, gentlemen?” Mitya shrugged sullenly and looked down. “I’ve never hidden how I felt. The whole town knows it—everyone in the tavern knows. Just lately I declared it in Father Zossima’s cell.... And that same day, in the evening, I beat my father. I nearly killed him, and I swore before witnesses that I’d come back and kill him.... Oh, a thousand witnesses! I’ve been shouting it for the past month, anyone will tell you so!... The fact stares you in the face, it speaks for itself, it cries out. But feelings, gentlemen, feelings are another matter. You see, gentlemen”—Mitya frowned—“I think you have no right to question me about feelings. I know your office binds you, I quite understand that, but that’s my affair, my private, intimate affair. And yet ... since I haven’t hidden my feelings before ... in the tavern, for instance, I talked to everyone, so ... so I won’t make a secret of it now. You see, gentlemen, I understand there are terrible facts against me in this business. I told everyone I’d kill him, and now, suddenly, he’s been killed. So it must have been me! Ha ha! I can make allowances for you, gentlemen, I really can. I’m thunderstruck myself, because who could have murdered him, if not I? That’s how it comes out, isn’t it? If not I, who could it be, who? Gentlemen, I want to know, I insist on knowing!” he exclaimed suddenly. “Where was he murdered? How was he murdered? How, and with what? Tell me,” he asked quickly, looking at the two lawyers.
“We found him in his study, lying on his back on the floor, his head smashed in,” said the prosecutor.
“That’s horrible!” Mitya shuddered. He put his elbows on the table and hid his face in his right hand.
“Let us go on,” Nikolay Parfenovitch put in. “So what drove you to this hatred? I believe you have stated in public that it came from jealousy?”
“Well, yes, jealousy. And not only jealousy.”
“A quarrel over money?”
“Yes, over money, too.”
“There was a dispute over three thousand roubles, I believe, which you claimed as part of your inheritance?”

“Three thousand! More, more,” cried Mitya hotly. “More than six thousand, more than ten, maybe. I told everyone, I shouted it at them. But I made up my mind to settle for three thousand. I needed that three thousand desperately ... so that packet of notes for three thousand, which I knew he kept under his pillow, ready for Grushenka, I counted as simply stolen from me. Yes, gentlemen, I regarded it as mine, as my own property....”
The prosecutor gave the investigating lawyer a meaningful look and managed to wink at him on the sly.
“We will return to that later,” the lawyer said quickly. “You will let us make a note of that point and write it down: that you regarded that money as your own property?”

“Write it down, by all means. I know that’s one more fact against me, but I’m not afraid of facts, and I bring them up against myself. Do you hear? Do you know, gentlemen, you take me for a different sort of man from what I am,” he added, suddenly gloomy and downcast. “You have before you a man of honor, a man of the highest honor. Above all—don’t lose sight of this—a man who has done a lot of nasty things, but who has always been, and still is, honorable at bottom, deep inside. I don’t know how to put it. That’s exactly what’s made me miserable all my life: I longed to be honorable, I was, so to speak, a martyr to the sense of honor, hunting for it with a lantern, the lantern of Diogenes. And yet all my life I’ve done filthy things like all of us, gentlemen ... that is, like me alone. That was a mistake, like me alone, me alone!... Gentlemen, my head aches ...” His brows drew together with pain. “You see, gentlemen, I couldn’t stand the sight of him. There was something ignoble in him, something shameless, that trampled on everything sacred, something sneering and irreverent, loathsome, loathsome. But now that he’s dead, I feel differently.”
“What do you mean?”
“I don’t feel differently, but I wish I hadn’t hated him so.”
“Do you feel remorse?”
“No, not remorse, don’t write that. I’m no great prize myself, I’m not very beautiful, so I had no right to find him repulsive. That’s what I mean. Write that down, if you like.”
Saying this, Mitya became deeply mournful. He had grown gloomier and gloomier as the inquiry went on.

Just then another unexpected scene took place. Grushenka had been removed, but not taken far. She was only in the second room along from the blue room where the examination was being held. It was a small room with one window, just past the large room where they had danced and feasted so lavishly. She sat there with nobody beside her but Maximov, who was terribly dejected and terribly frightened and clung to her side as if for protection. One of the peasants, with a metal plate on his chest, stood at their door. Grushenka was crying. All at once her grief was more than she could bear. She leapt up, flung out her arms and, with a loud wail, ran out of the room to him, to her Mitya. It was so sudden that nobody had time to stop her. Mitya heard her cry, trembled, jumped up and, with a yell, dashed to meet her, not knowing what he was doing. But they were not allowed to come together, though they could see each other. Men seized him by the arms. He struggled and tried to break free. It took three or four of them to hold him. She was seized too, and he saw her reaching out her arms to him and crying aloud as they carried her off. When the scene was over, he came to himself again, sitting in the same place as before, across from the investigating lawyer, and calling out to them:
“What do you want with her? Why do you torment her? She’s done nothing, nothing!...”
The lawyers tried to calm him. About ten minutes passed like this. Finally Mihail Makarovitch, who had been out of the room, came in hurriedly and said to the prosecutor in a loud, agitated voice:
“She’s been taken away, she’s downstairs. Will you let me say one word to this unhappy man, gentlemen? In your presence, gentlemen, in your presence.”
“By all means, Mihail Makarovitch,” the investigating lawyer replied. “In this case we have no objection.”

“Listen, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, my dear fellow,” the police captain began, and on his flushed face was a look of warm, almost fatherly feeling for the unlucky prisoner. “I took your Agrafena Alexandrovna downstairs myself and handed her over to the landlord’s daughters. That old fellow Maximov is with her the whole time. And I comforted her, do you hear? I comforted her and calmed her down. I explained to her that you have to clear yourself, so she mustn’t hinder you or depress you, or you might lose your head and give the wrong evidence. In a word, I talked to her and she understood. She’s a sensible girl, my boy, a good-hearted girl. She wanted to kiss my old hands and beg me to help you. She sent me herself to tell you not to worry about her. And I have to go, my dear fellow, I have to go and tell her you’re calm and easy in your mind about her. So you must be calm, do you understand? I was unfair to her. She is a Christian soul, gentlemen, yes, I tell you, a gentle soul, and not to blame for anything. So what am I to tell her, Dmitri Fyodorovitch? Will you sit quietly or not?”

The kindly police captain said a great deal that was out of order. But Grushenka’s suffering, the suffering of a fellow human being, had touched his good heart, and there were tears in his eyes. Mitya jumped up and rushed toward him.

“Forgive me, gentlemen, oh, allow me, allow me!” he cried. “You have the heart of an angel, an angel, Mihail Makarovitch. I thank you for her. I will, I will be calm, cheerful even. Tell her, out of the kindness of your heart, that I am cheerful, perfectly cheerful, that I’ll be laughing in a minute, knowing she has a guardian angel like you. I’ll have finished with all this very soon, and the moment I’m free I’ll be with her, she’ll see, let her wait. Gentlemen,” he said, turning to the two lawyers, “now I’ll open my whole soul to you. I’ll pour it all out. We’ll wrap this up quickly, wrap it up cheerfully. We’ll laugh about it in the end, won’t we? But, gentlemen, that woman is the queen of my heart. Oh, let me tell you that. That one thing I’ll tell you now.... I see I’m among honorable men. She is my light, she is my holy one, and if only you knew! Did you hear her cry, ‘I’ll go to my death with you’? And what have I done for her, a penniless beggar? Why does she love me so? How can a clumsy, ugly brute like me, with my ugly face, deserve a love like that, so that she’s ready to go into exile with me? And how she fell at your feet for my sake, just now!... and yet she’s proud and has done nothing! How can I help adoring her, how can I help crying out and rushing to her as I did just now? Gentlemen, forgive me! But now, now I’m comforted.”

And he sank back in his chair, hid his face in his hands and burst into tears. But they were happy tears. He pulled himself together at once. The old police captain looked very pleased, and so did the lawyers. They sensed that the examination was entering a new phase. When the police captain went out, Mitya was positively gay.

“Now, gentlemen, I’m at your disposal, entirely at your disposal. And if it weren’t for all these petty details, we’d understand each other in a minute. There I go again with the details. I’m at your disposal, gentlemen, but I tell you we must trust each other, you me and I you, or there’ll be no end to it. I’m saying this for your sake. To business, gentlemen, to business, and don’t rummage in my soul. Don’t pester me with trifles, but ask me only about facts and what matters, and I’ll satisfy you at once. And damn the details!”
So spoke Mitya. The interrogation began again.
